key_cases.case_name: Tyner v. Department of Social & Health Services, Child Protective Services
key_cases.holding: The court held that RCW 26.44.050 impliedly creates a negligent-investigation cause of action in favor of a child's parents, including parents themselves suspected of abuse, and that a later judicial no-contact order does not automatically break legal causation unless all material information was placed before the court.
key_cases.relevance: A biased or incomplete investigation that produces a founded finding and separation is actionable against the State.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that under RCW 26.44.050, CPS owes a duty of care to a child's parents, even those suspected of abusing their own children, when investigating allegations of child abuse.

key_cases.case_name: Ducote v. Department of Social & Health Services
key_cases.holding: The court held that stepparents are not within the class protected by RCW 26.44.050 and therefore lack standing to bring a negligent-investigation claim, limiting the protected class to children, parents, guardians and custodians.
key_cases.relevance: A stepparent stigmatized by a founded finding has no statutory negligent-investigation remedy, however damaging the finding.
key_cases.quote: they are not included in the categories of persons who may sue for negligent investigation under RCW 26.44.050

key_cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers and DSHS have only qualified, not absolute, immunity for reporting and investigating child abuse and for placing names on the central registry, and that the good-faith condition of the RCW 26.44.060 immunity is a question of fact.
key_cases.relevance: Holds that listing a person on the central registry after a founded determination is not protected by absolute immunity.
key_cases.quote: The determination of good faith under RCW 26.44.060 necessarily presents issues of fact.

key_cases.case_name: Costanich v. Department of Social & Health Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: In a case against Washington DSHS the court held that deliberately fabricating evidence in civil child abuse proceedings violates Fourteenth Amendment due process where a liberty or property interest is at stake, but granted qualified immunity because that right was not clearly established when the 2001 investigation occurred.
key_cases.relevance: Holds that a caseworker who deliberately falsifies the record supporting a founded finding violates due process.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that deliberately fabricating evidence in civil child abuse proceedings violates the Due Process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment when a liberty or property interest is at stake

key_cases.case_name: Hardee v. Department of Social & Health Services
key_cases.holding: The court held that due process is satisfied by the preponderance of the evidence standard in an administrative proceeding revoking a home child care license, and that the review judge's findings were supported by substantial evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the evidentiary standard and due process analysis governing administrative adjudication of child-safety findings against an individual.
key_cases.quote: Due process is satisfied by application of the preponderance of the evidence standard to the revocation of a home child care license, as provided by RCW 43.215.300(2).
